Pressure Washing in Grapevine, TX

Grapevine has old brick on Main Street and 25 miles of lake shoreline. Both call for restraint: less pressure on the walls, and no soap in the drains.

Lake first: where Grapevine's wash water goes

In Grapevine, pressure washing runoff can reach the same lake that helps fill your tap.

The city's stormwater plan says northern drainage flows to Lake Grapevine, with 25 miles of the lake's shoreline in Grapevine. The city has 65.3 miles of creeks as well. And about 30 percent of its drinking water comes from that same lake.

So the question of where the water goes has a direct answer in Grapevine. On a job in the northern part of town, soapy water at the curb is heading for the lake. Ask for a wash plan that uses plain water where it can, and collects anything with a cleaner in it.

Old brick on Main Street needs a soft touch

Grapevine has a designated Main Street Historic District, and its city site publishes the Secretary of the Interior's Standards.

What the standards say

Standard 7 says chemical or physical treatments, if appropriate, will be undertaken using the gentlest means possible, and treatments that cause damage to historic materials will not be used.

What the masonry guidance adds

The full federal guidance, posted by the City of Fort Worth, lists high-pressure water as not recommended on historic masonry. It suggests low-pressure water, detergent and soft brushes, tested on a small area first.

If you own or manage a building in the historic district, talk with the city's historic preservation staff before any wash. Ask what they will want to see.

Three Grapevine jobs, three different plans

Tasting rooms and shops

Sidewalks and entries before opening. Spilled drinks and foot traffic need a rinse more often than heavy pressure.

Homes near the lake

Shade can favor green growth on north walls. Keep any cleaner away from drains and banks.

Offices and hotels

Parking and entries on a set schedule. See the commercial page for what to require in a quote.

Before you call

Think about access too. Older buildings can share walls and walks with a neighbor, so tell them when work is planned.

Know whether your property drains north to the lake, and whether it sits inside a historic district. Mention both. Know what the walls and walks are made of, and say if the job is a roof, since a soft wash calls for a separate plan. Then read house washing or driveway cleaning, and see the cost guide.

An automated assistant answers at any hour. It transfers you to an independent company, which sets the price and does the work.

Creeks in the rest of town

Not all of Grapevine drains to the lake. The city's plan also names Cottonwood Branch, Denton Creek, the Elm Fork of the Trinity, Big Bear Creek and Little Bear Creek among the waters around it. Wherever your property sits, the path is the same: from the gutter into a storm inlet and on to one of those creeks, with no treatment on the way.

For a home, a plain water rinse steered onto the lawn is usually the simple answer. For a business with grease or oil, the water should be collected. Do not count on a drain near a building to lead to a sewer, because many outdoor drains do not. Grapevine's plan lists individual residential vehicle washing and street wash water among allowable discharges, but that is not a blanket approval for commercial washing with cleaners. If you are not sure, call Public Works at 817-410-3330 before work begins.

Check the company yourself. The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation's program list does not include power washing, and this site found no Texas state license for it, so you may have no state license number to look up. Ask for a certificate of insurance instead, ask how the wash water will be kept out of storm drains, get the price and scope in writing, and look up the business name on the Texas Comptroller's account status search (new tab). A sole proprietor may not appear, so a missing result does not by itself mean a problem. Dallas Power Washing Pro does not run these checks for you.

Common questions

Can a Main Street building in Grapevine be pressure washed?

Ask first. Grapevine's page on the Secretary of the Interior's Standards says treatments should use the gentlest means possible and that treatments that cause damage will not be used. Those are the words to take to the city's historic preservation staff before you hire anyone.

Where does Grapevine's water come from?

About 70 percent comes from the Trinity River Authority, supplied by Cedar Creek and Richland Chambers reservoirs. About 30 percent comes from Lake Grapevine.

Who do I call about a discharge in Grapevine?

Public Works at 817-410-3330 in operating hours. After hours, the city lists police dispatch at 817-410-8127, or 911.

Are there rules for watering in Grapevine?

Irrigation of any lawn or landscape is prohibited from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The city's Drought Contingency Plan is in Chapter 25 of its code, Section 25-140. Ask the city if a drought stage affects a wash.

Does all of Grapevine drain into the lake?

No. The city's plan says northern drainage flows to the lake, and it also lists several creeks in other parts of town. Ask Public Works if you want to know the path for your property.

Can I wash a patio near the lake with soap?

Be careful. Water with cleaner should be collected, not left to run to a drain or the bank. Plain water steered onto grass is the simple choice.

Need pressure washing in Grapevine?

Call at any hour, say what needs washing and which city it is in, and your call is transferred to an independent local power washing company with a short spoken summary. That company looks at the job, sets its own price and does the work.
